summary.description: The `summary` section: ONE short English paragraph, beginning with a square-bracketed task-type prefix. For this bundle the reference plates guide generation without being concrete frames, so the prefix is normally `[reference generation]`; add ` + audio reference` only if a voice or music reference is actually supplied. Summarise the target video, its subjects and its shot flow using the `<Subject N>` labels -- do NOT introduce new reference labels here, and do not restate the plate definitions.

detailedDescription.description:
MINIMUM 1900 CHARACTERS (~315 English words) -- this floor is enforced, not advisory. The guide asks for 350-500 words and measured g4-meromero output came in at ~206 words (1266 chars) even after the instruction was strengthened, so the length is enforced by the schema instead: llm.generate validates with ajv INSIDE its retry loop and, on failure, sends the model its own draft plus the specific error, which is a far easier task than hitting a length from cold. Do not pad -- reach the length by covering, FOR EVERY SHOT, all seven of: composition and framing; each subject's appearance AND position in frame; the environment and its light; the action as a state change (a beginning state and an end state); the camera motion; the sound in that moment; and where a referenced subject actually appears or takes effect. That is ~120-200 words per shot.
The `detailed_description` section -- the main body, and the only place shot-synced sound and dialogue belong. Normally 350-500 English words; do not pad to hit a count, and do let a dialogue-dense scene run long enough to fit the whole spoken timeline.
FORMAT, from the official guide:
  * Open with ONE OR TWO English sentences establishing the style and look, BEFORE the first shot marker.
  * `[Shot 1]` marks the opening shot and takes NO timestamp. Every later shot is `[Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, the shot cuts to ...` with a STRICTLY INCREASING cut time inside the duration. Use `the camera cuts to` / `the shot cuts to` / `the shot transitions to`; a cut must introduce new information about subject, space, state, viewpoint or time -- if only distance or a slight angle changes, use camera motion instead.
  * Write camera motion as natural English inside the shot using the controlled vocabulary: Zoom In/Out, Push In/Pull Out, Pan Left/Right, Truck Left/Right, Tilt Up/Down, Pedestal Up/Down, Arc Shot, Tracking Shot, Static Shot, Shake Slightly/Strongly, POV, Roll Clockwise/Counterclockwise -- optionally `with small amplitude` / `with large amplitude` and `at slow speed` / `at fast speed`, omitted when medium/normal. Never stack these as labels at the end of a sentence.
  * Cite `<Subject N>` at each subject's first clear appearance and keep using the same label afterwards. NUMBER THEM IN THE ORDER YOU LIST `references[]` -- the renderer emits subject_definitions in that order and remaps your labels if routing changes it.
  * SPEAKERS AND DIALOGUE: give each vocal source a stable `(S1)`, `(S2)` id, compound `(S1,S2)` when they speak together. Put the identifying phrase, action and delivery OUTSIDE the tag and only the language tag plus the exact words INSIDE: `<Subject 2> (S1) turns and says: <d>[English] I get off at the next station.</d>`. Preserve the authored line's words and punctuation verbatim, in its original language. For voiceover use the exact phrase `says in an off-screen voiceover` and immediately state that the character's lips remain closed. Use `<scenetrans>` on both sides of a line that crosses a cut, and `<cutoff>` when speech is truncated by the video ending.
  * On-screen text that is genuinely visible goes in English double quotes, verbatim.
Do NOT write ambience or audience-only score here -- those are the other two sections. Do not repeat dialogue outside `<d>`.

overallSoundscape.description: The `overall_soundscape` section: 1-4 English sentences in ONE paragraph summarising ambience, physical action sounds and non-verbal human sounds across the whole video -- wind, rain, traffic, footsteps, fabric, impacts, breathing, laughter, panting. Dialogue, singing and diegetic music belong in detailed_description and must NOT be repeated here. Use `N/A` only if complete silence is genuinely wanted.

nonDiegeticMusic.description: The `non_diegetic_music` section: 1-3 English sentences describing score the characters cannot hear. State instrumentation, speed, rhythm and dynamic change -- NOT abstract mood words and not the emotional function. Music a character can hear (radio, phone, someone singing) is diegetic and belongs in detailed_description instead. Use `N/A` when there is no score.

shotStructure.description:
THE DIRECTORIAL DECISION for this scene, made from the beat -- NOT inherited from how many shots the planner budgeted (that number is a duration split). The planner's shots are BEATS; three beats can be one continuous move.
There are THREE values, not two, because 'one continuous take' and 'the camera moves' are separate facts and pretending otherwise produces an incoherent scene -- a take marked continuous with a static camera gets you neither the cut nor any camera work:
  'continuous_moving' = ONE unbroken take in which the CAMERA TRAVELS and does the work a cut would do -- a half-orbit past a shoulder that reveals the second character, a push-in onto a face, an arc that swaps the background behind someone, a rack focus that hands attention across a room. cameraMove MUST name that travel.
  'locked_single'     = ONE unbroken take with a DELIBERATELY STILL camera. Legitimate only when the scene is a SINGLE sustained beat with nothing else that must be seen -- a held portrait, a landscape, one gesture. If the scene needs to show more than one thing and the camera will not move, it is not this.
  'multi_cut'         = two or more shots joined by described cut events.
CHOOSE 'continuous_moving' when: one location, unbroken time, at most two characters, a single escalating emotional beat, physical continuity matters, or intimacy and unbroken truth are the point and a cut would let the audience off the hook.
CHOOSE 'multi_cut' when: scale contrast IS the point, time passes, the location changes, an action has distinct impact beats, comedic timing needs the cut, or you are covering an exchange in shot/reverse. TWO CHARACTERS TALKING IS multi_cut BY DEFAULT -- an exchange has to see both faces, and only a camera that TRAVELS between them earns 'continuous_moving' instead.
CHOOSE 'locked_single' only for a genuine one-beat held shot.

references.description: The reference plates H3 holds identity from for THIS whole scene. ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: subjects first, most important first, and the single `location` reference LAST. HARD CAP 9 (H3's real limit, nearly double LTX MSR's 5) -- but fewer is still better, because every extra plate dilutes the others; cite only what is actually visible somewhere in this scene. Never empty. Appearance STATES are substituted automatically: when a character's ledger state has changed by this scene, the renderer swaps in that state's EDITED plate -- always cite the plain character id, never invent a state id. Because the whole scene renders in ONE pass, a character can only be held from ONE plate here: if their appearance changes mid-scene, cite the state they END in and carry the change itself in the prose.

id.description: MUST exactly match a story_bible id: a `characters` id for type 'character', an `objects` id for type 'object', a `locations` id for type 'location'. An id matching nothing is dropped with a warning and that subject is reinvented from scratch.

type.description: 'character' resolves against the per-character anchor plates (auto-substituted with this scene's appearance-state plate when one exists). 'object' resolves against the per-object anchor plates -- use it only when the scene's action is physically ABOUT that object (held, caught, carried, handed off, dropped). 'location' resolves against the per-location plates and is moved LAST; include exactly one per scene.

appearsAs.description: A SHORT (3-8 word) visual descriptor of what this plate shows, reflecting the character's CURRENT ledger state -- for 'character', stated gender plus one or two defining features ('elderly hunched fisherwoman in a green sari'); for 'object', its current visible state ('cane basket, half full of silver fish'); for 'location', the place and its light ('the fish dock at first light'). The renderer reads this straight into the '<Picture N> -- <appearsAs>' binding clause, so it must read as an identifying description, not a name.

job.description: What this plate is FOR in this scene, as a phrase that completes 'Use it for ___'. This is H3's single highest-leverage instruction -- assigning every reference an explicit job measurably beats handing the model images and a description. Be specific and DIFFERENT per plate: 'the woman's face, build and wardrobe, held identical across every cut' / 'the basket's exact weave, colour and size whenever it is in frame' / 'the location, its architecture, set dressing, palette and light'. Do NOT write a slot number here -- the renderer numbers the plates itself.

retention.description: How faithfully this plate is held, using the guide's FIXED English markers. 'fully_preserved' for an anchor plate whose identity must not drift (the normal case). 'partially_preserved' when some defined characteristic deliberately changes. 'attribute_transfer' when its characteristics move onto a different subject. 'weak_reference' when only broad style/category/atmosphere similarity is kept -- typical for a style or mood plate. Omit to default to fully_preserved.

duration.description: Seconds this scene runs, 5 to 15. H3 renders 5-15s per call and this whole scene is ONE call, so this is the hard budget every cut has to fit inside -- the renderer clamps anything outside it and snaps the result to H3's 17k+5 frame grid at 24fps, so small deviations are normal. Aim at the section's own budget; if the section's beats genuinely cannot fit in 15 seconds, cut the least essential beat rather than overrunning.

purpose.description: What this scene is FOR in the story -- the single beat it lands.

description: Scene prompt for MiniMax H3 in OFFICIAL full-reference format (MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3 docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_ref_en.md + _base_en.md). The model authors FOUR of the six sections; the RUNNER injects subject_definitions and retention_analysis at their fixed positions, because both are functions of the FINAL reference order after subjects-first/location-last routing and the 9-ref cap -- which the author cannot know. That is also why these are separate fields rather than one prose blob: subject_definitions PRECEDES summary, so the runner interleaves rather than prepends. Earlier revisions used a `<Picture N>` binding clause for every plate; that was WRONG -- the guide reserves <Picture N> for images acting as a concrete frame anchor and says an image used only to define a character, scene, costume or style must instead be cited inside a <Subject N> definition. LENGTH KEYWORDS HAVE A HARD CEILING in llama.cpp's JSON-schema-to-GBNF converter: it expands min/maxLength into that many character repetitions, and past a limit the grammar no longer parses -- the call then 400s with 'Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar' BEFORE generating anything, so it is a hard failure and not something a retry can fix. Bisected on this box: minLength 1950 ACCEPTED, 2000 REJECTED. minLength is therefore pinned at 1900 (~315 words), deliberately under the cliff, which is why it sits just BELOW the guide's 350-word floor -- the schema cannot enforce the full range on the local path. NEVER add maxLength at all (any value bloats the grammar the same way). And never add a non-standard top-level key such as _comment: local llama.cpp ignores it but OpenRouter rejects it outright with 'strict mode: unknown keyword'.
